title: Sublinear-seed generators for AC0 with parity gates
formal:
Do there exist two deterministic multitape Turing machines \(R,G\) with the following properties? For all integers \(d,a,n\ge1\), the machine \(R(1^n,1^d,1^a)\) outputs an integer \(r(n,d,a)\in\{0,\ldots,n\}\), and, for each seed \(z\in\{0,1\}^{r(n,d,a)}\), the machine \(G(1^n,1^d,1^a,z)\) outputs a string \(G_{n,d,a}(z)\in\{0,1\}^{n}\). For each fixed pair \(d,a\), both computations take at most \(K_{d,a}(n+1)^{b_{d,a}}\) bit steps for some constant \(K_{d,a}>0\) and integer \(b_{d,a}\ge1\), uniformly over all seeds. The seed length satisfies
\[
\forall d,a\ge1\ \forall\eta\in\mathbb Q_{>0}\ \exists N\ge1\ \forall n\ge N:
\qquad r(n,d,a)\le\eta n.
\]
For every \(n,d,a\ge1\) and every circuit \(C\) on \(n\) input variables with depth at most \(d\), at most \(n^a\) gates, and the gate types defined below, require
\[
\left|\Pr_{z\sim U_{r(n,d,a)}}[C(G_{n,d,a}(z))=1]
-\Pr_{x\sim U_n}[C(x)=1]\right|\le\frac1{10}.
\]
Here \(U_t\) is the uniform distribution on \(\{0,1\}^{t}\). The constant distinguishing error is the documented interpretation of the source question.
why: This asks whether an explicit generator can save an asymptotically complete fraction of the random bits against shallow circuits that freely combine Boolean operations and parity. It isolates a substantial gap between lower bounds for a well-studied circuit class and unconditional, efficiently generated pseudorandomness for that same class.
status_note: Source-open under the explicitly documented constant-error interpretation. Hatami–Hoza revision 2 of 14 April 2023 states the sublinear-seed challenge; its numbered sentence omits an error value, and this card selects error 1/10 from the surrounding constant-error setting. The individual source review and bounded later-work check on 16 September 2026 found no matching resolution. Restricted-gate and large-field results do not establish this target; this is not an exhaustive current-openness certificate.

progress.text: Corollary 4.18 gives a polynomial-time generator with seed length \(n-n/(\log n)^c\) for bounded-depth circuits with parity gates, saving a sublinear number of random bits while retaining linear seed length.
Revision 2 retains Open Problem 4.3.1, asking for explicit seed length sublinear in the output length.
Kumar posts improved generators and correlation bounds for structured models and circuits with restricted numbers of symmetric or threshold gates.
Cohen, Doron and Goldgraber post optimal-seed generators over fields of sufficiently large size and characteristic; their theorem does not include the binary-field regime.

sentences: These shallow Boolean circuits may combine AND, OR and parity gates throughout the circuit, with arbitrary reuse of input variables.
The question asks for one uniform generator that fools every circuit of each fixed depth and polynomial size with distinguishing error at most one tenth.
The generator must write all its output bits in polynomial time and use a seed whose length divided by the output length tends to zero.
The fixed error is an explicit interpretation of the source’s constant-error discussion because the numbered question does not specify an error value.
Known linear-seed savings and generators for restricted gate patterns or large-field polynomials do not meet this unrestricted parity-circuit target.

definitions:
A circuit is a finite directed acyclic graph with one designated output. Each input node is labeled by a literal \(x_i\) or \(1-x_i\), for \(i\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), or by a constant \(0\) or \(1\). Every other node is an AND, OR or PARITY gate with a positive, finite, unrestricted number of incoming wires. A PARITY gate outputs the sum of its incoming Boolean values modulo two. Gates and inputs may have unrestricted fan-out, and variables may be used repeatedly. The size counts AND, OR and PARITY gates, including the output if it is a gate, but not the literal or constant nodes. Depth is the maximum number of gates on a path from an input node to the output; a literal or constant output has depth zero. There is no restriction on the number, placement or successive layers of parity gates beyond the total size and depth bounds. The circuit class is nonuniform: the guarantee is for every individual circuit, with no requirement that its description be produced by an algorithm.

The generators receive unary \(n,d,a\), separated by delimiters, and \(G\) also receives the seed as an ordinary binary string. The seed-length machine \(R\) writes \(r(n,d,a)\) in binary. There is one finite program for \(R\) and one for \(G\), shared by every parameter triple; choosing a separate program or advice string for each output length is not allowed. All input reading, seed-length computation, preprocessing, arithmetic and writing of all \(n\) output bits are charged in the bit-cost bound. There is no oracle, advice or additional randomness. The polynomial runtime constants may depend on the fixed circuit depth \(d\) and size exponent \(a\), but not on \(n\), the seed or the particular circuit. The machines are not given a circuit description.

The seed condition is little-\(o\) for each fixed \(d,a\): the ratio \(r(n,d,a)/n\) tends to zero with no prescribed rate. It does not demand a bound \(n^{1-\delta}\) for a fixed \(\delta>0\), nor a bound uniform when \(d\) or \(a\) grows with \(n\). The probability spaces in the displayed guarantee consist solely of the independent uniform choices indicated in their respective experiments. The seed is not exposed to the circuit. The required error is the fixed rational number \(1/10\), rather than an error tending to zero or an additional small-error parameter.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of the existence of the two finite algorithms, their polynomial bit-cost bounds for each fixed depth and size exponent, the entire little-o seed guarantee and the fooling inequality for every permitted circuit, or a complete Lean proof of the logical negation of this proposition. A conditional construction, a nonuniform existence argument, a construction requiring superpolynomial time for fixed depth and size exponent, or guarantees only for a restricted arrangement or number of parity gates do not settle this target.

context_blocks.text: Open Problem 4.3.1 asks for an explicit sublinear-seed generator for constant-depth polynomial-size circuits with parity gates. The source leaves the error unspecified in that sentence; its immediately preceding discussion identifies the constant-error regime. This card fixes error 1/10 as an explicit interpretation and does not claim an inverse-polynomial-error version. Definition 1.4.1 and Section 1.4.1 supply full-output polynomial-time computation and a single uniform generator across parameter values.

The 2013 construction of Fefferman, Shaltiel, Umans and Viola uses seed length \(n-n/(\log n)^c\) for an appropriate constant \(c\), with error tending to zero against the relevant bounded-depth circuits. Although this saves many random bits, its seed-to-output ratio tends to one, so it does not satisfy the present little-\(o\) target.

The 2025 extractor-based results treat several structured models, including circuits with a restricted budget of symmetric gates. Parity is a symmetric operation, but those restrictions are not the unrestricted polynomial-size parity-gate model of this card.

The February 2026 optimal-seed result for polynomials imposes sufficiently large field size and characteristic. Its theorem does not cover the binary field, and the paper separately identifies the binary-field regime as a major remaining challenge; it is not a resolution for these Boolean circuits.

Read Fefferman–Shaltiel–Umans–Viola, On Beating the Hybrid Argument, final 2013 Theory of Computing PDF, Table 1 and Corollary 4.18 with its proof on pages 833–834. The bound is n(1-1/log^c n) and remains Theta(n), while still achieving a nontrivial additive saving. Corollary 4.8 is for odd characteristic and was not substituted for the actual parity-gate Corollary 4.18.

Read Kumar arXiv:2501.02653v1 abstract and Section 1.1, pages 4–5. Its symmetric-gate count restrictions and other structured models were kept separate from arbitrary polynomial-size AC0[parity] circuits. Full proofs were not independently audited.

Read Cohen–Doron–Goldgraber arXiv:2602.10030v1 Introduction, Definition 1.1 and Theorems 1.2–1.3. The actual positive theorem requires q=Omega((d log d)^4/epsilon^2) and characteristic Omega(d^2); the statement does not apply to binary polynomials of growing degree. Its small-field theorem is a conditional reduction. Full proofs were not independently audited.
